title: A Three-Party W-State Quantum Secret Sharing Protocol with X-Gate Encoding and Forbidden-Outcome Detection
authors: Timur R. Teregulov, Elena R. Loubenets
abstract: We develop a new three-party quantum secret-sharing (QSS) protocol based on a three-qubit W state. This protocol encodes the secret-sequence bits using X gates and employs randomly selected Hadamard operations and measurement bases to generate information and security-test rounds. We evaluate the efficiency of the proposed protocol and analyze its security against an internal adversary performing intercept-and-resend and entangle-and-measure attacks, deriving the corresponding detection probabilities. The analysis of the entangle-and-measure attack shows that extracting information through an ancillary system leads to a nonzero probability of forbidden outcomes in the test rounds, thereby enabling the detection of the attack. The proposed protocol is implemented in Python using the Qsikit framework and executed on quantum processors. Its performance is evaluated in terms of the quantum bit error rate (QBER) for information rounds under different secret-bit encoding configurations. The experimental results demonstrate that the QBER depends noticeably on the quantum processor used.
summary: This work introduces a three-party Quantum Secret Sharing protocol utilizing the W state and X-gate encoding for secure bit distribution. It analyzes the protocol's efficiency and proves its security by demonstrating that an eavesdropper attempting to gain information will inevitably cause detectable errors during security test rounds. The protocol is implemented and tested on quantum processors.
main_problem: The paper develops and analyzes a novel three-party Quantum Secret Sharing (QSS) protocol based on the W state to securely distribute a secret quantum bit.
main_result: The protocol is shown to be secure against internal adversaries because any attempt to gain information (entangle-and-measure attack) results in a non-zero probability of detecting the intrusion via forbidden outcomes.
method: The protocol uses X-gate encoding on a three-qubit W state, incorporates random Hadamard operations, and involves distinct information and security-test rounds for verification.
model_or_system: The system is a three-qubit quantum state initialized in a W state. Operations include X-gate encoding, random Hadamard gates, and measurements performed in randomly chosen bases (Z or X).
key_observables: Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER), detection probabilities for specific attacks, and the probability of an informational round ($P(R_i \in I) = 5/12$).
important_parameters: The efficiency is quantified by the qubit efficiency ($\eta_q \approx 13.89\%$), and performance is noted to depend on the specific quantum processor used.
main_assumptions: The security analysis focuses on internal adversaries, and the efficiency calculations assume uniform probability over all combinations of gate applications and measurement bases.
figures_summary: Table 1 illustrates quantum states resulting from X-gate applications and the corresponding secret bits. Table 2 summarizes round types based on Hadamard applications and measurement bases. Figure 1 shows the circuit for one protocol round.
paper_structure: The paper details the protocol construction using the W state and X-gate encoding, analyzes its efficiency by calculating round probabilities, and rigorously proves security by analyzing the detection probability against intercept-and-resend and entangle-and-measure attacks.
why_interesting: The rigorous security analysis, particularly the link between information gain and detectable disturbance (forbidden outcomes), provides a concrete, experimentally verifiable measure of security for quantum communication protocols.
